chapter: Church, Creole life and Mobile musicians
title: Creole language and the Creole people of Mobile
summary: He talks about older Creoles speaking French, the broken French of Mon Louis Island, and his mother's and wife's French families.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Had your father played any music? No, no, no. He didn't play any music? No, no. He was just a common laborer. One other question, and then I'll stop, is about the Creole people here. Did they speak the Creole dialect or any language, you know, like French?

Well, some of them did, yeah. The older heads did. But, and coming up in the late days, they didn't take much interest in teaching their children. Did they have any special Creole songs in Creole? Do you remember? Down in Mononville Island they speak it, yeah. They call it the Broken French down there. Which island? Mononville Island. That's just about 18 miles down the road, yeah. Out in the Bay, then. Mononville Island, yeah. I guess you've read of Dauphin Island. Well, it's right, right to the side of Dauphin Island. And the people over there that speak that Creole. Yeah, and the Creole people practically owned the whole island at one time, but now they're sold on several land, but there's many of them down there yet. That's where most of my wife's people's from.
But the Creole people, are they mostly French or some Spanish?

Yeah, they're mixed with French and all. Now, my mother, I've been there as I can learn, she came from down in Nassau somewhere, and she spoke French good. My mother was really speaking French. And her mother, she came from Bordeaux, France, my wife's mother. Bordeaux, France. And that's it, they spoke French good. But the younger ones, the people of Mononville Island, they kept the broken French, I believe. They called it the regular Creole talk down there, and they didn't speak it down there yet. But in the city, yeah, they dropped it somewhere or another, you know, they carried on with their children, so their children never knew. And the undercoastered line, a few words, you know. Bonsoir and so on. Well, we certainly enjoyed talking. Can we shut your mouth and all sorts of things?
